# Harm Reduction in the Time of Monsters

## The POWER Act and Me

*“The old world is dying, and the new world struggles to be born: now is the time of monsters.” ― Antonio Gramsci*

I open with this (somewhat apocryphal) quote because I believe it perfectly encapsulates our present moment. Capitalism has reached yet another crisis and again returns to the well of fascism to maintain its grip on power.  I cannot blame those who look around and assume that our only recourse is down a road there is no coming back from; but to believe this, one has to give up on any hope of a better world being possible through other means. I don't believe this strain of thought benefits anyone. So long as any other avenue remains, it should be explored. There are many systemic issues that won't be solved by legislation alone, and ultimately implementing socialism will be the answer to those lingering issues. But, there are still levers we can demand our government pull to mitigate and protect us from the harm caused by unregulated capitalism. HB5513/SB4016, otherwise known as the **P**rotecting **O**ur **W**ater **E**nergy and **R**atepayers (POWER) Act, is one of those levers. The POWER Act may not go far enough in the opinions of some, but it is the best option currently on the table  to rein in the unregulated proliferation of data centers in our communities, one of the latest ploys by creeps like Zuckerberg, Bezos, and Ellison to extract yet more value from our labor and tighten the noose of fascism by enabling their surveillance state. In our struggle for victory, we cannot lose sight of measures that will provide amelioration of the conditions of the working class. In short: harm reduction is based.

One of the most accessible issues with the proliferation of data centers  is the impact it has on our energy bills. I am sure we have all been shocked at the price of our ComEd bills compared  to last year. The Citizens Utility Board   recently published figures that show ComEd rates are up 40-50% from just two years ago\! Industry experts are laying the blame  squarely at the feet of data center developments. ComEd is a part of the Regional Transmission Organization (RTO) called PJM Interconnection. PJM manages the interconnected grids for northern Illinois (ComEd) and all or part of 11 other states and  the District of Columbia. To ensure that there is adequate capacity within the grid, PJM holds annual auctions of the energy planned to be produced . All projects  projected to be connected to the grid are taken into account when these auctions take place. Because data center developments are largely speculative in nature, many of the data center projects may never actually be built but still need to be *assumed* as true when determining prices for the finite supply of energy available in the RTO. These increased prices impact all levels of the grid, from local distribution  to the plants providing the energy. We  see this trickle all the way down to  your ComEd bill.

### **So how would the POWER Act help us?**

First, it would (1) require utilities to create new policies to protect consumers from subsidizing data center related transmission and distribution infrastructure upgrades to the grid, (2) require data center developers to foot the bill for their interconnection costs, and  (3) require that data center-related price increases from PJM are passed to data centers and not other consumers. Second, a policy framework within the POWER Act known as BYONCE (Bring Your Own New Clean Energy) would incentivize developers to come to the table with their own supply of renewable energies. Developers that provide proof they will  back their projects with local, renewable clean energy—certain percentages of supply need to be met by key dates to qualify—would see an expedited path to interconnection and would not be subject to the energy curtailments during periods of peak demand that data centers that *do not* bring their own clean new energy would face. The POWER Act would establish guardrails to steer price increases away from everyday consumers and save us from the "wild west."

Another  issue when it comes to data centers, particularly the hyper-scaled variety, is the water usage associated with cooling and powering their hardware. Previous generations of hyper-scaled data centers could consume millions of gallons of water *a day*. Increasingly, we are seeing that newer data centers are opting to use closed-loop cooling as they come under increased scrutiny regarding their impact on local water supplies. Closed-loop cooling technology is presented as being more water-conscious than open-loop evaporative cooling. At face value, this is true, but the benefits aren't as large when you begin to factor in their increased energy consumption .These closed-loop systems also consume millions of gallons when they are first filled, and this is not just a one-and-done process. These systems need to be filled and flushed numerous times after assembly to ensure the plumbing is cleared  of debris caused by the assembly process.  Recently,  the waste water from one of these  data center flushes in Cheyenne, Wyoming was not treated properly prior to being flushed into the city's waste water system, which is reused throughout the city to provide water for sprinkler systems in parks and golf courses.  The warm moist environment in these cooling systems requires anti-biological additives to prevent biological contamination of the system, and testing confirmed an outbreak of *Cupriavidus gilardii* within the Cheyenne waste water.  An investigation traced the outbreak back to  improperly-treated flush water from a Meta data center.

Once filled and running, these systems still need to be flushed and refilled about every 10 years. The liquid running through the system once operational is about 75% water and 25% Propylene Glycol, an anti-corrosive and anti-freeze additive. Questions still remain about the long term impact on our waterways from these chemicals. The POWER Act  introduces reporting and efficiency requirements that will help mitigate the harms outlined here. For example, data centers will be required to transparently publish their water consumption and local water supply impact. The Illinois State Water Survey will be required to review each data center's specific water use plan and likely impacts on the region. The Illinois Environmental Protection Agency  would be  prohibited from  issuing any permits if evaluations confirm that a data center will have adverse impacts on water resources.

The environmental harms of unregulated data centers are the more "in your face" issues associated with this fight, but you would also be hard-pressed to find a more clear example of the fascism creeping into everyday life in America. All across the country we see the same stories:  communities standing together to voice their opposition to a local data center while their municipal government holds backroom meetings with the developers and pushes these proposals through,  ignoring their constituents. Data center developers also force municipal governments to sign non-disclosure agreements prior to engaging with them in negotiations for a data center proposal. This leaves communities in the dark and subverts the democratic process, putting profits over people. Those with the most to lose will inevitably end up the most impacted when these deals are realized. The POWER Act would prohibit municipalities from signing onto these NDAs with data center developers. It would also ensure that there are open and transparent community benefits agreements  between the developers and the municipalities in which they will be built. This ensures that the working class people in our communities see these benefits, such as funding for school systems, when a data center is built there; not just kickbacks for corrupt city councils.

### **Timeline**

There has been extensive debate over the POWER Act since the spring:

* **Feb 11:** Sen. Villivalam and Rep. Gabel introduced their respective sides of the bill.  
* **March:** Proponents and advocacy groups held press events and urged action to move the bill out of committee.  
* **April 15:** The Illinois House Executive committee held a  subject matter hearing that brought together opponents and proponents for the bill to debate.  
* **Late Spring:** Additional committee meetings were held  to debate  the bill  
* **May 30:** Environmental coalitions and hundreds of advocates rallied at the Illinois State Capitol to lobby representatives and senators,  but ultimately not enough votes were secured to bring this to a vote in the Spring. Citing this inaction, JB Pritzker took executive action to suspend the data center tax credits and urged that statutory guardrails be passed.

Over the summer, WSIL DSA and other groups have been advocating for Illinois State Senators and Representatives to bring this to a vote in the fall legislative session.  The POWER Act will give a shot in the arm to our renewable energies industries and ensure that the data centers that do get built are responsible partners in growth for our state.

### **So how can you get involved?** 

The easiest step you can take is to fill out our handy [Action Network letter writing campaign](https://actionnetwork.org/letters/pass-the-power-act?source=WSILstop&) that matches you with your state Senator and Representative and sends them a prewritten statement that urges them to bring this to a vote in the fall, and thanks them for their support if they are already a cosponsor. Once you've sent your letter, share the campaign with your friends and family\! Your next step is joining your local DSA chapter and organizing with them to stop the unregulated spread of data centers.

**Already a member?** Join your chapter's anti-data center efforts, and if they don't have anything going, then start organizing\! We need to get everyone in Illinois onboard with pushing our elected officials to action. Every voice matters and we *will* build a better world together\!
